item.title: No critical slowing down in the Atlantic Overturning Circulation in historical CMIP6 simulations
item.dc:creator: Maya Ben-Yami, Lana Blaschke, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, sea surface temperature, Earth system, model intercomparison, CMIP, ensemble
by Maya Ben-Yami, Lana Blaschke, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a key component of the Earth’s climate system, and has been suggested to have multiple stable states. Critical slowing down (CSD) can detect stability changes in Earth system components, and has been found in sea-surface temperature (SST) based fingerprints of the AMOC. Here, we look for CSD in historical simulations from 27 models from the sixth Climate Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6). We calculate three different CSD indicators for the AMOC streamfunction strengths at 26.5°N and 35°N, as well as for a previously suggested SST-based AMOC index (ASSTI) based on averaging SSTs in the subpolar gyre region. No model shows CSD in the ASSTI, which is in marked disagreement with observations. This lack of CSD is reflected in the AMOC streamfunctions in most models, although individual ensemble members in some models do show signs of CSD even under a conservative significance calculation. We thus conclude that: 1) The historical AMOC in CMIP6 models is not losing stability, 2) studies of AMOC stability should consider an ensemble of realisations, 3) there is no non-AMOC-related physical process in CMIP6 models which could cause signs of CSD in North-Atlantic SSTs in the 1850–2014 period, and thus the CSD in the observed ASSTI is likely a sign of a change in the AMOC. This final result suggests that observed changes in the ASSTI could indicate a loss of stability in the real-world AMOC.

item.title: Antarctic sea ice over the past 130 000 years – Part 2: A review of its role in the Earth system
item.dc:creator: Zanna Chase, Karen E. Kohfeld, Amy Leventer, David Lund, Xavier Crosta, Laurie Menviel, … (+9)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, sea ice, ocean circulation, proxy, carbon cycle, Earth system
The impacts of recent dramatic declines in Antarctic sea ice on the Earth system are uncertain. We reviewed how sea ice affects ocean circulation, ice sheets, winds, and the carbon cycle by considering theory and modern observations alongside paleo-proxy reconstructions. We found evidence of connections between sea ice and these systems, but also conflicting results, pointing to missing knowledge. Our work highlights the complex role of sea ice in the Earth system.

item.title: Nonlinear longitudinal stress coupling in glacier and ice sheet flow
item.dc:creator: Logan Elliott Mann, Katarzyna Warburton, Colin Meyer
item.category: Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Sciences
item.description:
Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Sciences — matched: ice sheet, basal friction/drag, glacier, Antarctic, Greenland
Abstract The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets exhibit high variability in flow speed, over multiple orders of magnitude. This flow integrates forcings from complex, multi-scale and spatially heterogeneous pressure gradient and friction fields into smooth and continuous flow fields, over a finite scale known as the longitudinal coupling length (LCL). The strongly nonlinear, shear-thinning rheology of ice complicates the stress transmission, but previous work has relied on either linear (Newtonian) models or linearized, small-perturbation models, to determine the coupling length. Here, we derive new exact solutions to the nonlinear shallow shelf/shelfy-stream approximation (SSA), which explain how nonlinear feedbacks between the stress state and the nonlinear rheology of ice determine the coupling length. For complex and multi-scale flow fields, these exact solutions provide a foundation for Green's function approximations that can reconstruct the effects of a non-local stress balance, given input data for the driving stress and friction fields. This allows us to rapidly reconstruct the ice velocity field, asses changes in basal drag and interpret the effect of rheology on shear margins.

item.title: Stratigraphic Signals and Cloudy Band Chemistry in Ice Cores Revealed by Large‐Area Elemental Mapping
item.dc:creator: Pascal Bohleber, Piers Larkman, Rémi Dallmayr, Martin Šala, Nicolas Stoll
item.description:
Geochemistry Geophysics Geosystems — matched: Antarctica, Greenland, polar, meltwater, ice core
Abstract Mapping the impurity distribution in 2D with laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA‐ICP‐MS) has provided valuable insights into the micro‐chemistry of a broad range of environmental samples. However, technical limitations have largely restricted mapping to millimeter‐sized maps as “snapshots.” Especially for stratigraphic archives with layers on the cm to mm scale and finer, much could be gained from increasing the map size to encompass the layer scale. Polar ice cores are a prime example of this: They are invaluable climate archives, but detecting impurity‐related climate signals in highly thinned ice is a state‐of‐the‐art frontier. Here we introduce a new methodology using LA‐ICP‐MS that allows chemical mapping over large areas (cm × cm) within a feasible measurement time (<1 h). For validation, we used “cloudy bands” from Greenland and central Antarctica: visual stratigraphic layers characterized by high impurity concentrations. Our large‐area maps show clear bands of high intensities at positions of cloudy bands. The large maps let us take advantage of the merit of 2D data for feature recognition: Stratigraphic layers can be identified at sub‐mm detail that would be missed by standard 1D meltwater analysis. Large‐area mapping delivers important new insights for both understanding ice‐impurity interactions and reliably detecting climate signals in highly deformed deep ice. As such, it will be a key component for future high‐throughput analysis of hundreds of meters of ice cores. Ultimately, the new methodology provides a vital “bigger picture” in LA‐ICP‐MS mapping, opening important new applications for the study of other environmental samples.

item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: satellite altimetry
This study presents a high-resolution wave energy resource database across 11 maritime regions for the period 2011–2023. Using satellite altimetry, sea wave parameters were obtained and validated against wave buoy and ERA5 data. The results provide a geospatial database for the development of marine renewable energy technologies and sustainable coastal planning, supporting the transition toward specialized offshore engineering solutions.

item.title: Evaluations of Precipitation, Temperature, and Circulation Characteristics in Simulations of CMIP6 Models over the Arabian Peninsula
item.dc:creator: Raju Pathak, Hari Prasad Dasari, Caspar M. Ammann, David N Yates, Ashok Karumuri, Ibrahim Hoteit
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Earth system, CMIP, ensemble
Abstract This study evaluates the performance of 74 CMIP6 (including HighResMIP) models for the historical climate of the Arabian Peninsula (AP). The analysis examines whether models reproduce the mean climate, trends (accounting internal-variability), extremes, and key circulation/process diagnostics. Despite strengths, several limitations persist across key aspects. Precipitation biases include annual-mean wet-bias over the southern AP and dry-bias over the central AP, and models underestimate the frequency and intensity of heavy-precipitation-events. Temperature simulations show high-pattern agreement, but nearly all models exhibit wet-season cold-bias and misrepresent the hot- and cold-tails. Distribution diagnostics indicate that inter-model-spread dominates uncertainty and that ensemble-means can be sensitive to outliers in extreme analyses. Precipitation biases covary with pressure-gradients, Red Sea flow/convergence, synoptic-transients, and jet-structure; while dry-season biases are dynamically consistent with a monsoon-desert linkage diagnosed using ω500, the tropical-easterly jet, and Tokar-gap related flow. Coarse-topographic representation in models weakens winds and moisture transport, but its impact is also subject to season, variable, and orographic height. Paired within-family runs further show that higher-resolution and added Earth-system-complexity can improve AP fidelity in some configurations but can also yield neutral or degraded performance, indicating that resolution is beneficial but not sufficient for robust skill. No single model excels across all diagnostics, but a combined phenomenology-process-framework identifies high-skill models while flagging cases where strong composite performance may mask weak process realism or bias compensation. These results provide an observationally-constrained basis for model selection and uncertainty characterization, underscoring the need for rigorous validation and continued model improvement for reliable regional-climate projections.

item.title: Artificial intelligence pathways from weather to climate
item.dc:creator: Tom Beucler, J. David Neelin, Hui Su, Shivanshi Asthana, Chris Bretherton, Will Chapman, … (+7)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: emulator, ensemble, downscaling
arXiv:2610.09770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning has made rapid advances in weather forecasting: autoregressive models trained on atmospheric reanalyses now rival dynamical models across nowcasting, medium-range, and subseasonal-to-seasonal lead times, producing well-calibrated ensemble forecasts at reduced cost. We review these advances and consider their extension to climate horizons, where the challenge shifts from initial-condition skill to producing reliable statistical responses under altered forcings. AI-powered climate prediction systems must produce credible forced responses to drivers (e.g., greenhouse gases, land-use change) typically outside the observed record. We propose two minimum requirements for AI in climate modeling: (i) external forcing agents must enter explicitly enough to support interventions in which they vary independently; and (ii) robustness must be stress-tested in out-of-distribution regimes, including extremes and counterfactual trajectories. Using leading AI autoregressive emulators and hybrid physics-AI models, we identify development and coupling challenges. Comparing the reported throughput of these models with that of GPU-ported dynamical models highlights how AI can reduce time-to-solution by advancing only the target variables at the required resolution and using longer time steps, rather than integrating a full high-frequency, multivariate state. Diverse AI downscaling strategies can partially substitute for explicit fine-scale resolution, paving the way toward inexpensive local hazard assessment across prediction horizons.

item.title: Historical climate extremes in Europe and the connection between spring precipitation and summer heat
item.dc:creator: Laura Lipfert, Ralf Hand, Angela-Maria Burgdorf, Christian Pfister, Heinz Wanner, Stefan Brönnimann
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: climate extreme
We analyse the link between dry springs and hot summers in Europe over the past 600 years. Starting with a study of the heat summer of 1473, which followed dry spring conditions in Southeastern Europe, we use the ModE-RA data set family to statistically analyse the link. We find that the link is strongest in regions where evaporation is moisture-limited. Hot summers are preceded by increased blocking over north-central Europe and a positive East Atlantic pattern in spring.

item.title: Trans-CAUNet: a swin transformer-based network for automated mapping mountain glaciers from multisource remote sensing imagery
item.dc:creator: Wenlin Huang, Huiyuan Luo, Yang Liu, Qiang Xu, Chuanhao Pu
item.description:
International Journal of Remote Sensing — matched: glacier, remote sensing
Accurate and automated extraction of glaciers is pivotal for water resources and ecological systems in the cryospheric. Given the expanding access to remote sensing imagery, there is an urgent requirement to develop efficient methods to identify glaciers in High Mountain Asia (HMA). Proposed here is a novel UNet-based model embedding the Swin Transformer and channel attention mechanism (CAM) parallel modules. This design effectively captures global-local and contextual information from multisource imagery, further enhancing spectral features. Trained on a dataset from three regions, it achieved impressive results relative to other popular deep learning models and distinguished glaciers from similar terrain elements, with an F1 score of 0.93 and a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 0.87. Besides, it demonstrated robust transferability when applied to more challenging glacier environments in Southeastern Tibet. The proposed model presents a viable solution for the rapid and accurate monitoring of glaciers dynamics.

item.title: Closing Data Gaps in Regional Glacier Trends of the Wind River Range, Wyoming, USA
item.dc:creator: Massimiliano Clayton, Yingkui Li
item.description:
Glacies — matched: glacier, snowpack
Glaciers in Wind River Range, Wyoming, have experienced substantial reductions in surface area and volume in recent decades, yet existing inventories contain temporal gaps and often mix glaciers with seasonal snowpack. We mapped and classified glacier outlines using high-resolution satellite imagery in 2006 in Google Earth Pro (version 7.3.7.1327) and compared them against inventories from 1963–1974, 2015, and 2020. A classification approach was applied to distinguish glaciers from snowpack based on Welch’s t-test of significant difference in elevation changes within and surrounding mapped outlines based on four digital elevation models from 2000 to 2019. Results show an 11% decrease in mapped glacier/snowpack features from 1963–1974 to 2006 (476 to 423), with a 21% reduction in mapped outlines classified as glaciers (314 to 247). Total glacier area declined from 48.35 km2 in 1963–1974 to 34.06 km2 in 2006, while volume decreased from 0.998 km3 to 0.701 km3. From 1963–1974 to 2015, area and volume losses reached 47% and 49%, respectively, consistent with accelerated regional retreat. An unusually low reduction observed from 2015 to 2020 is likely caused by methodological inconsistencies between existing inventories. This study underscores the need for standardized mapping protocols and robust classification between glaciers and snowpack to accurately document glacier changes and assess their impact on water resources.

item.title: Snow cover variability in the Western Beskids (Poland) during the 1951–2023 winter seasons
item.dc:creator: Agata Drabek, Alicja Biesmer, Damian Absalon
item.description:
Scientific Reports — matched: abrupt change, climate change
Abstract The impact of long-term snow cover variability on winter tourism in the mountainous areas of Poland is an increasingly important research topic, particularly in light of the anticipated effects of climate change. Available studies are often of regional scope, limited to higher elevations, while lower mountain ranges such as the Western Beskids remain insufficiently studied. This study aims to examine trends, determine the rate of change, and identify abrupt changes for selected snow cover variables: snow cover duration [SCD], total number of days with snow cover equal to or greater than 30 cm [SCD ≥ 30], and potential snow cover duration [PSCD]. We show that during the study period, the seasonal duration of snow cover decreased at approximately half of the studied locations, while no significant trends were observed for skiing-specific indicators. The most pronounced downward trends occurred in January and March. At the same time, step change detection revealed abrupt changes in time series, mostly in the 1980s. Our results demonstrate that snow cover variability can be effectively assessed in lower mountainous regions and in climatically complex temperate zones, provided that sufficiently long time series are available. They also confirm that the declining trends in snow cover observed elsewhere are likewise present in the Western Beskids.

item.title: Global warming and the National Cattlemen’s Association 1986–1996
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Jacquet, Loredana Loy
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: global warming
by Jennifer Jacquet, Loredana Loy In the mid-1980s, scientific studies first highlighted the role of anthropogenic methane in global warming and emissions from cows as an important source. This knowledge expanded views of responsibility for global warming beyond the fossil fuel sector. Using scientific studies, archival documents, media interviews, and various government reports, we analyzed how the National Cattlemen’s Association (NCA), a trade association for the U.S beef industry, reacted to news about its products’ impacts on global warming between 1986 and 1996. While previous studies have emphasized the role of trade associations in political lobbying, here we show that NCA responded mainly with strategic communications, including information gathering on civil society activities, commissioning academic experts to produce and share statistics that reframed scientific findings, and discursive tactics to influence politicians and the public. Despite scientific recommendations about opportunities to reduce methane emissions, we found no evidence that NCA researched or promoted any of these suggested changes to beef production. Instead, NCA treated global warming as a public relations concern that could affect consumer demand, rather than as a potentially serious consequence of beef production.

item.title: Pysammos 1.0.0: a discrete-to-continuum transformation Python tool to analyse the rheology of granular materials
item.dc:creator: Claudia Elijas-Parra, Eric C. P. Breard, John P. Morrissey, P. J. Zrelak, Mark Naylor
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Granular flows are widespread in nature and industry, yet poorly understood. Discrete particle simulations offer detailed insight into their behaviour, but only provide properties of the individual particles, such as velocity and force. To obtain bulk flow quantities relevant to science and engineering, such as pressure or strain rate, we present Pysammos: an open source, user-friendly too to process discrete particle simulation data into continuum fields.
